blocks.text: Isaiah 58 challenges a form of worship that seeks God through fasting while leaving oppression, conflict, and unmet need untouched. The chapter defines the fast God chooses in concrete communal terms: freeing the oppressed, sharing food with the hungry, housing those without shelter, and clothing the naked. Sabbath observance belongs within this same vision of honoring what is holy rather than pursuing one’s own advantage.

The chapter’s promises of light, guidance, healing, and restoration are tied to the transformation it describes. Its concern is not merely whether people perform religious acts, but whether their life together reflects justice, release from oppression, and care for vulnerable people.

The Great Isaiah Scroll is an almost complete witness to all sixty-six chapters of Isaiah. It broadly aligns with the Masoretic tradition, though it contains many spelling and substantive differences; other Isaiah manuscripts from Qumran also show that the book was actively copied and interpreted. The nature and significance of particular differences remain disputed.
